title: Multipliers
author: Liz Wiseman
theme: The best leaders do not rely on their own brilliance; they amplify the intelligence and capability of the people around them.
summary: Liz Wiseman spent years developing leaders at Oracle and noticed that some managers left their teams sharper and more energised, while others, often equally talented, left people drained and holding back. Her research, drawn from interviews and studies of well over a hundred leaders, sorts them into two types. Diminishers treat intelligence as scarce and assume people cannot work things out without them. Multipliers believe people are smart and will grow when stretched, and as a result they get far more out of the same team, roughly twice as much by her estimate.

She describes five disciplines that separate the two. Multipliers act as talent magnets, attracting capable people, using them at their full ability and helping them move on to bigger roles, whereas empire builders hoard staff and underuse them. Multipliers are liberators who create a safe but demanding space where people think and speak freely; tyrants create anxiety that shuts thinking down. Multipliers are challengers who set ambitious questions and let others find the answers, instead of know-it-alls who issue directions. They are debate makers who involve people in rigorous discussion before major decisions, rather than deciding alone. Finally, they are investors who hand over real ownership and hold people accountable, instead of micromanagers who take control back at the first sign of trouble.
Wiseman stresses that diminishing is often accidental. Well-meaning leaders who rescue people, jump in with ideas or talk with constant enthusiasm can quietly signal that others need not think.

The good news, she argues, is that multiplying is a learnable mindset rather than a fixed trait. Leaders can start by building on one existing strength, experimenting with a single new practice, asking questions more than giving answers, and noticing which of their own habits cause others to hold back.
takeaway: Measure your leadership by how much capability you draw out of others, not by how smart you appear yourself.

questions.q: What core belief distinguishes Multipliers from Diminishers?
options: Multipliers believe strict control produces the best results
Multipliers assume people are smart and will figure things out
Multipliers think only a few stars matter
Multipliers believe intelligence is fixed at hiring
questions.why: Multipliers start from the assumption that people are capable and will grow when challenged, while Diminishers see intelligence as scarce.

questions.q: Roughly how much more capability does Wiseman estimate Multipliers get from their people?
options: About ten percent more
About the same amount
About twice as much
About ten times as much
questions.why: Her research suggested Multipliers draw roughly double the capability from people compared with Diminishers.

questions.q: Which role is the Multiplier counterpart of the Empire Builder?
options: Talent Magnet
Liberator
Investor
Challenger
questions.why: Talent Magnets attract and fully use capable people, while Empire Builders hoard resources and underuse them.

questions.q: What does a Liberator create for the team?
options: A relaxed space with no expectations
A chain of approvals for every idea
A competition in which only the best idea survives
A safe yet demanding environment where people think freely
questions.why: Liberators remove fear while still asking for people's best thinking and work.

questions.q: How does a Challenger differ from a Know-It-All?
options: The Challenger gives more detailed instructions
The Challenger sets stretching questions and lets others find answers
The Challenger avoids setting goals
The Challenger only works with senior staff
questions.why: Challengers define opportunities and hard questions, whereas Know-It-Alls tell people what to do.

questions.q: What does a Debate Maker do before an important decision?
options: Decides quickly alone to save time
Delegates the decision without discussion
Engages people in rigorous debate to test the options
Asks only for a vote by show of hands
questions.why: Debate Makers drive sound decisions by involving people in thorough, evidence-based discussion.

questions.q: Which behaviour marks an Investor rather than a Micromanager?
options: Giving people real ownership and holding them accountable
Stepping in to take over whenever problems arise
Checking every detail personally
Keeping key decisions with the leader
questions.why: Investors hand over ownership and expect delivery, while Micromanagers take control back.

questions.q: What does Wiseman mean by an accidental diminisher?
options: A leader who deliberately suppresses staff
A team member who undermines the boss
A leader who lacks technical skill
A well-intentioned leader whose habits unintentionally shut down others' thinking
questions.why: Good intentions such as rescuing people or offering constant ideas can still discourage others from thinking.

questions.q: According to the book, can leaders become Multipliers?
options: No, it is an inborn trait
Only after many years in senior roles
Yes, it is a mindset and set of practices that can be learned
Only if they change organisations
questions.why: Wiseman presents multiplying as learnable, starting with small deliberate experiments.

questions.q: Which simple shift does Wiseman suggest for leaders who want to multiply?
options: Make more decisions personally
Ask more questions and give fewer answers
Hire only experienced specialists
Reduce how often the team meets
questions.why: Asking questions invites others to think and contribute instead of relying on the leader's answers.
